Youngstown Sheet and Tube Co. v. Sawyer. The 1952 Steel Seizure Case held that President Truman lacked constitutional authority to seize steel mills threatened by a labor strike during the Korean War without explicit Congressional authorization. During the Korean War, steelworkers threatened to strike. Truman ordered Secretary of Commerce Sawyer to seize and operate the mills to maintain war production. The steel companies sued, arguing the President had no constitutional power to seize private property without Congressional action.

Justice Robert Jackson's concurrence articulated a three-tier framework for presidential power. The President's authority is greatest when acting with Congress, uncertain in a gray zone, and at its lowest point when acting against Congress. The majority held that only Congress has the power of the purse and can authorize extraordinary economic measures. The President cannot unilaterally seize property. The decision established that inherent executive power does not justify overriding property rights or substituting for Congressional authority. It became the leading case defining the limits of presidential power during emergencies and crises, reaffirming that no one, not even the President, is above the law.
